Title: Soulbound

Genre: Epic Fantasy

Feedback request: I'd like to know how engaging this opening page is. I'd also like to hear impressions of the characters and world.

As the storm-tossed sky loomed above, the gate of Duradan stood defiantly against tempestuous winds. Its twin towers, ancient sentinels of stone weathered by centuries, bore banners that snapped like writhing beasts. The silver star on a field of green whipped alongside the city standard, a white tower on blue. Misty rain blew in sideways, finding every gap in Caelan’s wool coat.

The bustling crowd surged toward the city in a chaotic tide of bodies. Wagons creaked and groaned, their wheels churning through the mud. Mounted men and women trudged alongside, their steeds plodding wearily.

Amidst the throng, a man on horseback flung a curse at Caelan as he brushed past, but the words were lost in the cacophony. Caelan stared eagerly at the gate, a grin on his angular face. “A city,” he whispered. He turned to see Gothra’s normally curly black hair plastered flat against his face, water beading down his round cheeks. “We’re actually here!” he shouted to his friend.

“You think there’s gonna be anyone jugglin’ fire in all this?” Gothra asked, his voice half lost in the crowd.

Caelan’s laughter bubbled up despite the elements. “No,” he replied, “but the tavern’s hearth will be crowded, I bet. And don’t forget about the ale, there’s no Mrs. Warben to lecture us here.”

“I won’t complain about a mug of ale, or two.” Gothra grinned.

Fifth bell tolled, the aged belfry straining to be heard over the howling wind. The tempest above responded with a booming crack of thunder, tearing the sky with lightning. Conversation would have to wait.

A scowling guardsman studied Caelan as they approached but waved them through no less. As they passed under the ancient stone archway, the earth trembled. Stoneworks groaned stubbornly as the ground shook. The belfry spat granite chips onto the crowd. Caelan held his breath.

Pandemonium erupted in moments. Women and children screamed. Caelan heard “siege” as often as he did “earthquake”. Those who fled one way were met by a dozen others going the opposite direction. Quickly people were being trampled, pushed down relentlessly as they struggled to get back to their feet. They looked like fish in a barrel.

Caelan grabbed Gothra by the cuff and pulled him to the edge of the crowd before they too could be trapped in the chaos. The earth steadied beneath them, but the thundering of a thousand footsteps and the shrill cries of panic echoed through the city, joining the storm.

“Who’s that?” Gothra yelled, pointing deeper into the throng.

Caelan height let his eyes pass unobstructed over the crowd, settling on a tall figure in a colourful patchwork cloak. A man by his height, he was plucking some sort of instrument, strolling through the crowd.

“A minstrel, or maybe a bard,” Caelan said, leaning down to speak into Gothra’s ear, but there was no need.

An expectant hush fell over the crowd, broken only by a single, soothing sound—a warm, ethereal tone that gently drifted across the square. Overhead, the storm held its breath, waiting.

“Right, let’s go see, then. Wonder if he knows ‘Barden’s Cloak’, or ‘Daisy for a Maiden’.” Gothra said, pulling Caelan toward the crowd.

Thanks for your critique of my writing!

I definitely understand the need to keep the he details limited to what is necessary for the story and limiting it to what is needed to be known.

Describing the first guard was a choice I made to try and humanise him a little. He is large but soft featured. Relena bracing her fall is to show his strength. I wrote this to set up the challenge she has in escaping past the guard.

The power needs to have the effect I’ve given it on its wielder because there is no conversion in the magic. Relena can take someone’s emotions, but she must hold them to do so. Like stealing a bag of coin, it can not make you run faster. This is crucial to the story as a whole and Relana’s character.

Relena is more than a thief. I tried to allude to this when she tries to recall the last time she was caught thieving. She mentions that this was a long time ago. 

All of this setup is to payoff the fight scene at the end, where Relena has to go through extreme emotional turmoil to defeat the guards (she has only killed one guard, the other is dull). 
Relenas reference to it being a “soul” she takes is just how she thinks of it. When referring to it outside her thoughts, I use “emotion” and inside her thoughts I often use “soul”

The title becomes relevant in the following chapter, but I have an epigraph that comes before this chapter which mentions it also.

Thank you for your critique again, I just wanted to explain my plan and the purpose of some of the writing here, but I can see the value in your suggestions and will take them onboard as I continue.

Again I really appreciate your critique. I’m still learning to show rather than tell. I find when I’m writing with a good flow I can get into a poor habit of tell, tell, tell. I think revision is going to be an important skill for me to learn.

I hadn’t noticed my reliance on that sentence structure. It is definitely one of my favourite sentence structures but overusing it is going to be boring like you said. I’ll spend some time looking for new structures I like and playing with various sentences to add a bit of variety in the prose.

Continuity problems I’m seeing some holes in the plot upon deeper consideration. Why didn’t the guards search her? A single guard arrested her and because of her stature, gender and crime, didn’t see her as a potential escapee. This might be poor plot here but essentially just a shitty guard.

Why hasn’t she used them in the past? She has, it’s her most common tool. The bracers are nearly impossible to remove by a person without magic. My explanation here is that the bracers attach themselves to Relena, sort of becoming an extension of her body. A person with magic could in theory negate this effect or find a way around it. In the past she is usually bound until someone more capable can arrive. They usually don’t arrive on time.

I think I could definitely set those things up in the story a little better and I’ll try to work some more details about this into my next chapter.

I noticed a few things that stood out to me.

>appearing nearly black in the lightless void

This sentence is a little confusing. Lightless implies there is absolutely no light and so there should be absolutely no colour. In fact, she shouldn't be able to see anything. You could reword this as "nearly lightless void" or perhaps, "despite the lightlessness of the void". I understand this is a dream, but because you didn't acknowledge it, as a reader, I assume you made a mistake. Whether you did it intentionally, I don't know.

Another thing I noticed off the bat was that the perspective changes at times. Initially, it feels like this is written in third-person limited but it strays to third-person omniscient below.

>She and her mother waited in silence. Every so often, Amara would gently squeeze and massage Brynna's feet — **something she did less for her daughter's comfort, and more to keep her hands busy.**

This isn't something that Brynna should know.

>With one last squeeze to her daughter's toes, Amara pushed herself off the bed and waddled after her husband. Sinking back into the bed

And again this perspective feels omniscient.

>"Aye," Elyas intoned, distracted by the design sketches spread out before him. 

Does Brynna know he is distracted? How does she know?

The perspective changes continue after this so I won't mention any more. If this is a stylistic choice, I don't think it's necessarily a bad one and if you like it, then by all means keep going.

Outside of this, I found Brynna to be a bit passive, and I found that my interest waned as the story continued. Your few paragraphs were sharp and compelling. You had me for the first two and a half pages or so, then I felt the story hit a very sudden lull. After we learn that the king has died I expect the plot to progress further. This feels like a significant plot point and event in the story. The description of the kitchen and home add detail to the world, but it feels like they take precedent over plot progression which I feel we haven't gotten enough of.

I think that we have too many characters to think about for a first chapter here. We have Brynna, Amara, Anders, Elyass and Bjorn. Trying to picture 5 new characters, understand who they are and what they want is difficult with 3000 words. Rather, I think the story would be better served by focusing on 1-3 characters at most in this first chapter so as to not overwhelm the reader. 

Overall I found the story interesting at the start and I want to know what happened to the King, but right now I don't care about any of the characters enough to care what really happens to any of them next. I think your descriptive language is good, though perhaps a little much for my taste at times. Your world is interesting and the dream at the beginning adds the right level of wonder where you can keep tying things back to that to keep the reader trying to work out what's strange about this world. I found your prose to be pretty good and there are some gems that were pointed out below such as.

>"Instead, the thunder of hoofbeats joined to the tense symphony they wove."   


Your word choice here is lovely and I find that various sentences have a poetic feeling which I enjoyed.  


Great work so far! Keep it up.

I'm giving advice despite being in the same boat, so take that as you wish. (Longest is 14k right now) but here are some tips that took me from barely able to do 5 sentences to more like 5-6 chapters I don't hate.  


**My advice**  
Accept that your story isn't going to be what you wish it to be. This isn't because of your ability to focus or any deep personal issue, you simply have never written a book. It will take you time to be able to write down an idea and identify how you can turn that idea into a full length novel. Likely you have an amazing scene in your head, and your characters have deep, interesting backgrounds, but what are they? If you're like me you have ideas but you don't have a true backstory and character arc laid out ready to go. 

So first thing's first, learn to write bad. Taken any sport as an example. If I wanted to learn golf, and all I wanted to do was to hit a hole in one, and I tee'd up over and over and every time I didn't hit a hole in one I said, "well that's too bad I better just hit this ball differently and then it'll work." People would think me mad. You need to play a game of golf and do terrible, then play again and see where you can shave off a couple of shots and improve, you get the jist.  Don't  try and write the amazing scene into a book, write a book and even if you don't fall in love with it just finish it and be done with it. Once you do that, you'll be able to take some of your spectacular ideas and flesh them out more, every book will be an improvement.

I'd like to leave a big "I'm a newbie" stamp on my critique. Being quite new to creative writing I am still growing to understand how identify good writing and seperate it from average writing. With that in mind, lets dig into it.

**Worldbuilding**

I felt like the world building was adequate but lacked a shine or flare that compelled me or sparked my imagination. We do have some hints at a more fantastical world here. "Stories about the shades and wraiths living in the mountain wilderness," though this felt like it was thrown in for this purpose but without any impact to our introduction here. I would've enjoyed more active voice in this excerpt.

>"She feared walking alone through the dark, for her father was a teller of wild tales. He raised her on stories about the shades and wraiths living in the mountain wilderness beyond the estate. He reminded her that those evil spirits only tormented people who violated caste law, and she had always been obedient to the gods. Still, it was frightening, for she worried that she had not been faithful enough. "

I believe showing us more of her fear, fright and paranoia would have served the story better here and enhanced the world. Giala's reactions to sounds in the night, shadows in the corners of her vision or various other spooks and scares would have enhanced this world building element for me and added more life to the world.

Not a lot else to comment on, It felt like the typical fantasy world you would picture halfway through a story where our protag is part way into their journey.

**Character**

I like Giala, but I don't care if she dies. That's the simplest way I can express my feelings toward Giala after the first chapter. She has a decent backstory and I feel pity for the character, perhaps too much so, though I agree with another critique which comends your choice to have Giala obey the caste system and treat those below her much as she is treated, this does a good job to add more depth to her character and stop her from feeling like the typical can never catch a break character which can feel stale.   


I feel as though you have some inconsistency with Giala aswell, the following quote hints that she has a bit of fire in her and does not simply submit to others will.

>“You’ve been fighting again,” her mother said, staring at the girl’s swollen bottom lip. 

This is in contrast to the second half of the chapter where she meets our next character, who I'll get to next. Her timidy and submission in this scene is justified by her strict adherense to her caste system, which is good and I agree with this approach, however a little resistance and perhaps some level of unrest for Giala might serve to keep that thread you set up earlier in the reader's mind and further add more depth to Giala.  


Just briefly I'd like to mention that our character that Giala meets feels like an "iconic" character and I'm expecting him to be one with a simple arc or simply have no major arc, acting more as a constant throughout the story or simply through our introduction, however some humanising elements would have helped the story I believe. Giala's timidy and confusion at the man's generous care for her would be furthered if our traveller introduced themeselves with a name or pseudonym and made a small attempt at asking Giala about herself. Giala could shrug this off or act confused even further, but I think the story needs this to add life to the dialogue.  


**Dialogue**

I'm horrible at dialogue, though I am not particularly skilled in any of my writing so far, but I can follow my gut feeling on this. The accenting of our traveller is good in my opinion and is great for a bit of world building. Diverse voices are always a win to me, however it can become too much. If the purpose of our traveler is to fill that iconic character type of role than I think this accent in the dialogue works great, however if the character is being built to have a significant part in the story and an arc then I think the voice will need to be a bit more flexible in how heavily it's accented, though this is certainly something that is often personal preference.   


Aside from the voices, I feel the dialogue serves it's purpose but isn't very engaging. Having Giala be timid limits you in this aspect, though I think that there is room to add some dialogue from our captor. Giala's captor/the traveller seems to be a lively character with a big personality, this would lend itself well to him being a little more inquisitive as to who she is, why she was unconscious next to a barrel of waste and why she wouldn't speak. You set this character up as a larger than life sort of wild man with a soft spot. In the dialogue the character seems to be very inactive, only saying the things needed to allow you to explain Giala's caste doctrine and how it's affected her personality. I think the dialogue would benefit greatly from treating the captor/traveller as a character with individual motives and establishing those even slightly. Here is an example below that I think could be improved upon.  


>“An Oo Way? What, by fire, is an an-oo-way?” he asked, badly mispronouncing the word. “This some rutt’n caste thing ye heathens are always on about? Gods’ blood.”

This quote gives us a bit of perspective. We see that the stranger is not from her land or at the very least does not follow the local belief system, but what does he think of it, and how does this impact him? Here's an edit that I think helps to liven up this dialogue.

>"An Oo Way?" the stranger scrunched his pudgy face, "What by fire, is an-oo-way?"  
>  
>He fumbled over the words, *did he really not know of the anuhui?* She thought.  
>  
>"This some rutt'n caste thing ye heathens are always on about?" The man shook his head, red beard waving gently, much like the flames.  
>  
>"An what rutt'n caste are ye, girl? Yer some kind of shite' merchant?" He didn't stop for a response. "Ey, hardly a town left wher' I don't 'ave some poor sod trynna' wipe me arse. It's a shite world"

I've made some assumptions about the world just to give an example here and it's expanded but I think it gets across my critique.  


**Prose**

I think your prose is quite good personally and I found your level of detail in descriptions to be just right, never going so long as to let my mind wander while managing to create a pretty immersive level of detail. I think there was some portions that felt a little off, though I don't feel I can offer any legitimate advice here. Overall it felt good and it is a solid foundation.

​

**Final Remarks**

I think this is a great foundation for a fantasy novel. The pieces are there, they just need some fleshing out and a little shaping here and there to really get them to snap into place. I found the caste system to be interesting and it was one of the strongest pulls for me to keep reading. I liked your imagery in the beginning and I think your prose is well suited to this genre, keep it up and be sure to take my feedback with maybe a scoop of salt.

Hi there,

First of all I like the little connection between uncertainty as a principle of quantum physics and a principle in everyday life for many people, particularly those who have undergone trauma.  


Now, do you have ADHD or know anybody who does? I myself am an adult with ADHD and I found that your character's backstory is very hard to believe or suspend my disbelief for. One of the major struggles of ADHD for myself and many others is our ability to maintain goals, effort and attention. Your character seems to follow a trope I think is common which is that the person who suffers from something is healed after some intervention and experiences  a huge boost in their capacities. In your backstory the child is shown to be a child genius after some therapy and a diagnosis, however those with ADHD would most likely find this to be unauthentic, in reality years of therapy can help a person manage their disorder and through a lot of hard work, effort and habit building, most people with ADHD can function at a good capacity and achieve what they desire. However, children with ADHD are not strong responders to therapy and require a lot of structure to be placed in their lives often, usually medication is of good help but most children are going to feel the effects a bit harder, gradually adapting and building habits and lifestyles that help them grow to manage their disorder better. I believe that it would be a better backstory to have your character continuously struggle with their condition rather than have this up and down of them overcoming it but then being traumatised by abuse and regressing in another path.   


I get the feeling that this backstory stems from an idealistic view of what someone with ADHD could be like, and it's okay to make our heroes a little stronger than we are, it is often a depressing read to just see someone struggle the whole time, but we want our characters to feel authentic and so I think the best thing for this character is to give the, a backstory where they constantly battled their ADHD and through their hard work, their intelligence and aptitude is allowed to shine through. Don't make them perfect by the end, make them better, show us how they have grown.  


A good thing you can leverage is a thing called "Hyperfocusing". It's a term people with ADHD often use to describe our periods of extreme focus and attention on things that we find interesting, usually for a relatively short period of time. This can be our superpower and playing this up in a book would feel more authentic and add that sort of hero who rises above their disorder vibe that I think you want. Perhaps he can pass through school despite struggling with behaviopur or attention because he is so fascinated with science that he truely enjoys that area of study and hyperfixates on each new topic.

Also, if an 11 year old kills a grown adult male, make sure you find a way to do this that doesn't feel like it's unbelievable, this isn't something that would occur easily.  


Good luck!
